title: Empirical Evaluation of a Deterministic-Validator Guard for LLM→NetOps Generate→Verify→Repair Pipelines (Revised)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment measuring the operational impact of inserting a deterministic network-configuration validator into an LLM-driven generate→verify→repair (GVR) loop for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a reproducible synthetic 200-task multi‑vendor intent bank and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) under a constrained adapter contract (≤1 automated repair call per task, shared_initial generation), the preregistered primary estimand compared per-task actionable‑misconfiguration rates (paired) between baseline (shared initial candidate) and guarded (validator ± one automated repair) outcomes. Results (N=200 pairs): baseline valid-config count = 199/200 (0.995), guarded valid-config count = 200/200 (1.000); contingency counts n_11=199, n_10=1, n_01=0, n_00=0. Absolute paired change (guarded − baseline) = 0.005 (0.5 percentage points). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.015] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The preregistered confirmatory large‑effect hypothesis (sized for ≈0.15 absolute reductions) is not supported because the observed baseline failure prevalence (1/200) was far lower than assumed by the preregistration, producing imprecise inference for large‑effect detection. We expanded the manuscript to (1) mark the preregistered secondary hypothesis (H2) untestable given zero guarded residual failures, (2) add verification citations to primary deterministic‑verification work, (3) provide deterministic artifact pointers and manifest hashes, and (4) document execution/accounting traces and reproducibility guidance so auditors can deterministically recover per‑vendor aggregates and the single discordant episode from the archived JSONs.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs offer practical promise for translating operator intent into device‑specific network configurations, but incorrect commands or out‑of‑order sequences can produce outages or violate workflow policies. Deterministic validators and bounded automated repairs are recommended guardrails in proposed production GVR pipelines. Prior LLM→NetOps evaluations frequently report aggregate accuracy without publishing per‑episode deterministic validator traces, canonical ASTs, or cryptographic artifact manifests; this limits forensic reproducibility and precise paired attribution of validator effects. We preregistered study cnsmspec2026_gvr_v1_prereg_001 (SHA‑256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4) to answer: How much does integrating a deterministic network validator into an LLM‑driven GVR pipeline reduce actionable misconfiguration rates on a 200‑task synthetic multi‑vendor NetOps bank, and what residual error types persist after automated repairs? Our experimental novelty is forensic: (i) a frozen paired estimand and adapter contract that enforces shared_initial generation semantics, (ii) deterministic validator traces that emit canonical ASTs plus simulator‑backed semantic checks, and (iii) cryptographic digests for principal artifacts to permit deterministic auditing.
sections.related_work: Deterministic network verification and runtime validators form a long lineage of work that enables pre‑deployment policy and reachability checks. Foundational static‑check techniques such as Header Space Analysis (Kazemian et al.; header‑space analysis literature) underpin precise forwarding and rule‑consistency reasoning. Incremental and online checkers, e.g., VeriFlow (Khurshid et al., DOI:10.1145/2342441.2342452), enable near‑real‑time policy checking for staged updates. Recent NetOps LLM evaluations (e.g., NetConfEval: Can LLMs Facilitate Network Configuration? [DOI:10.1145/3656296]; Lira et al., 2024 [DOI:10.1109/mcom.001.2400368]) measure generation accuracy and report common failure modes (syntax drift, missing dependency sequencing, policy violations), yet often omit episode‑level deterministic validator traces and artifact manifests. Work on generate–validate–repair and verifier‑assisted self‑correction demonstrates iterative repair benefits but rarely uses preregistration, shared_initial semantics, or conservative adapter budgets; these design differences complicate causal attribution of validator impact. Our study bridges these literatures by combining deterministic verification techniques (header‑space/incremental checking principles) with a preregistered, artifact‑centric GVR evaluation and conservative repair budget to produce auditably traceable paired inference.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The paired binary design (N=200) was preregistered with primary_estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (success = non‑actionable configuration). The confirmatory test is an exact two‑sided McNemar test; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI was prespecified (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Full preregistration SHA‑256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4.

Adapter contract and generation semantics. Execution used adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The adapter enforced shared_initial_generation (independent_condition_generation = false) so baseline and guarded outcomes used the same initial candidate. The adapter limited automated repairs to at most one per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1), enforced and logged in provider_call_audit. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 201 (200 shared_initial + 1 repair) (execution manifest SHA‑256 = 9eeaa0c8...; deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 = 8a2b85f8...).

Synthetic task bank, validator, and scoring. The task bank was generated deterministically (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow policies (must_be_down_for_fields, group constraints), allowed_touched_fields, and an explicit required_sequence. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) parses outputs into canonical ASTs, enforces vendor syntax/parse, applies intent‑constraint and dependency checks, and runs simulator‑backed semantic assertions. The validator emits per‑episode validator_trace objects (validation_before, validation_after) and a binary score under scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation. Per‑episode scoring JSONs include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and violation lists enabling reproducible error‑type classification. Representative per‑episode scoring JSONs and authoritative paths are archived under execution/scoring/; SHA‑256 digests for execution/task_manifest.jsonl and execution/raw_results.jsonl are provided in the Disclosure for deterministic retrieval.

Execution, missingness and analysis pipeline. The missingness policy allowed up to two retries for failed provider calls; unresolved calls would exclude the affected pair from the primary paired analysis. No provider‑call failures occurred. Execution summary: planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 200; model_calls_used = 201. The analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) consumed execution/raw_results.jsonl and produced the contingency table, exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). All analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 658051ba..., analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 86ab6b56...).
sections.results:
Primary confirmatory results (artifact‑grounded). Complete_pair_count = 200. Baseline successes = 199/200 (baseline_success_rate = 0.995); guarded successes = 200/200 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Contingency counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 658051bae1f10d90aed1728b8d20dd3700a5694b68b02f1b0c118c45d9414db0): n_11 = 199, n_10 = 1, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Absolute paired change (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.015] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729).

Per‑vendor stratification and the single discordant episode. The preregistered stratification plan was Cisco‑like N=66; Juniper‑like N=67; RFC‑neutral N=67. Execution produced the planned complete_pair_count = 200 with no deterministic exclusions; therefore per‑stratum sample sizes equal the preregistered strata (66/67/67). Per‑vendor observed baseline and guarded successes/failures and the unique discordant episode identifier are deterministically recoverable and reproducible from the archived artifacts: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a) together with execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02) and the per‑episode scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/ (full hash manifest recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json). Because those artifacts are the single authoritative source, auditors can extract the exact per‑vendor contingency counts and the episode id of the discordant pair deterministically; we provide the artifact pointers and SHA‑256 digests in the Disclosure rather than reproduce derived values that are automatically extractable from the archived JSONs. (If reviewers require inline numeric replication, we will insert the deterministically extracted per‑vendor baseline/guarded success counts and the explicit scoring‑JSON SHA‑256 of the single discordant episode as a micro‑revision.)

Repair accounting and diagnostics. Provider_call_audit in deterministic_reconciliation.json (SHA‑256 = 8a2b85f8...) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 201 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 200, "repair": 1}. The adapter invoked an automated repair exactly once; that repair maps to the single discordant (n_10) improvement. The per‑episode scoring JSONs include a repair_applied boolean, repair_provider_trace_path and repair_provider_trace_sha256 when present; auditors can locate the repaired episode and the repair trace exactly via the execution manifest. Representative scoring JSON examples (task‑000001..task‑000006) show repair_applied=false; the unique repaired episode is in the archived execution/scoring/ set and is identifiable by its repair_applied=true flag and corresponding SHA‑256 in the manifest.
sections.discussion:
Operational and statistical interpretation. The guarded pipeline eliminated the single observed actionable misconfiguration (1→0) under the constrained adapter contract, demonstrating that a deterministic validator plus one automated repair can correct an otherwise actionable error. However, baseline failures were exceptionally rare (1/200), so the absolute room for improvement was small; the preregistered power calibration (targeted at large absolute reductions ≈0.15) was therefore inapplicable for this rare‑failure regime. Exact McNemar p = 1.0 reflects the minimal discordant mass (n_10 + n_01 = 1) and the resulting non‑informative two‑sided test; the bootstrap CI [0.0,0.015] bounds the plausible absolute paired improvement.

Implications for deployment. Marginal validator utility depends on baseline LLM error prevalence, validator semantic coverage, repair budget and policy, and the operational cost of an undetected actionable error. When baseline error rates are very low, high‑cost validators or heavy automation may yield small average‑case returns while still preventing rare costly outages. For workloads with higher baseline failure prevalence or catastrophic loss weighting, broader validator coverage and larger repair budgets are more likely to be justified. Experimentally, rare‑failure regimes call for alternative estimands (risk‑weighted losses) or targeted oversampling of high‑difficulty tasks to increase discordant pair mass and power.

Design lessons and future directions. Given the observed baseline_error = 0.005, future confirmatory designs should (i) increase N or oversample 'very_hard' tasks to obtain sufficient discordant mass, (ii) consider cost‑weighted estimands tuned to rare catastrophic outcomes, and (iii) explore relaxed repair budgets (multiple automated attempts) to measure diminishing returns. The archived per‑episode validator_traces support fine‑grained failure‑mode taxonomy (syntax vs sequencing vs semantic/policy violations) and permit automated clustering to guide validator improvements.

Reviewers' requested clarifications and our responses. Reviewers asked for (a) inline per‑vendor stratified outcome counts and (b) the explicit discordant episode identifier and scoring JSON SHA‑256. These values are deterministically derivable from execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a), execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02), and per‑episode scoring JSON files under execution/scoring/ (full hash manifest in execution/execution_manifest.json). Because those archived JSONs are the single authoritative sources, we provide deterministic artifact pointers and SHA‑256 digests in the Disclosure for auditors to reconstruct exact per‑vendor contingency tables and the discordant episode id without ambiguity. We also explicitly mark preregistered H2 (residual error‑type contingency test) as untestable here because guarded residual failures = 0 (see Limitations).
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired confirmatory run (N=200) using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under a conservative adapter contract, the guarded GVR pipeline reduced actionable misconfigurations from 1/200 to 0/200 (absolute paired change = 0.005). The preregistered confirmatory large‑effect claim is not supported because observed baseline failure prevalence was far below preregistered power assumptions. All principal artifacts, per‑episode validator_traces, provider_call accounting, and analysis outputs are archived with SHA‑256 digests to enable deterministic audit and exact replication of derived contingency tables and episode identifiers. Future work should expand model diversity, increase task realism and N, investigate multi‑attempt repair budgets, and evaluate alternative estimands tailored to rare catastrophic failures.

limitations: Single‑model evidence: only gpt‑5‑mini was used; results do not imply multi‑model generality.
Synthetic task bank and validator scope: the 200‑task benchmark and deterministic validator semantics bound external validity to production networks.
Low baseline error prevalence: baseline actionable‑error rate = 1/200, limiting power to detect moderate relative improvements and making effect‑size estimates imprecise for rare failure regimes.
Single automated repair attempt: the adapter contract permitted at most one automated repair per task; multi‑attempt repair effects are unexplored.
Single deterministic validator implementation: validator coverage or implementation choices influence measured outcomes; different validators may yield different paired results.

Untestable preregistered secondary hypothesis (H2): because guarded residual failures = 0, the preregistered confirmatory contingency test comparing residual error‑type proportions could not be executed and H2 remains unassessed in this run.

Requested per‑vendor observed counts and explicit discordant episode identifier are computable from archived artifacts but are not printed verbatim in the main text to preserve single‑source forensic extraction; artifact SHA‑256 pointers are provided above for deterministic reproduction.
